items.prompt: Two processes both have a pointer with the same value, 0x7fff1000. Why doesn't reading through it in process A ever accidentally return data from process B?
choices: The OS randomizes pointer values so they never collide
Each process has its own page table — the same virtual address maps to a different (or no) physical location per process
Processes share physical memory directly, but the CPU blocks cross-process reads in hardware
It's mostly coincidence — occasionally it does leak data between processes
items.explanation: Addresses are never physical from a process's point of view. The MMU translates every virtual address through that specific process's page table, so identical virtual addresses in two processes almost always resolve to entirely different physical memory — often none at all.
items.reference:
🅰️ Process A

page table A

🅱️ Process B

page table B

Why: the same virtual address in two processes is translated through two independent page tables.
items.learnMore:
Virtual addresses aren't physical

Every pointer a process holds is a virtual address — a number that only means something once it passes through that process's own page table. The MMU (memory management unit) does this translation on every single memory access, not just occasionally.

When two processes both hold the value 0x7fff1000, that's a coincidence of numbering, not a shared location. Process A's page table maps it to one physical page; process B's page table maps it to a completely different physical page — or to nothing at all. Reading through a pointer never bypasses this translation, so there is no path by which A's data could show up when B reads 'the same' address.

This is also why concepts like shared memory (e.g. POSIX shared memory segments) have to be requested explicitly by both processes — the kernel has to deliberately map the same physical pages into both page tables. Isolation is the default; sharing is the opt-in.

items.prompt: Process X writes the string "secret" to virtual address 0x5000. Process Y, running at the same time, reads virtual address 0x5000. What does Y most likely get?
choices: "secret" — both processes are reading the same address
Whatever Y's own page table maps 0x5000 to, unrelated to X's write — very likely not "secret"
A permission error every single time, with no exceptions
Half of X's data, mixed with Y's own memory at that address
items.explanation: 0x5000 is only a number until it passes through a page table. X's page table and Y's page table almost certainly map 0x5000 to different physical pages (or Y's mapping may not even exist), so Y's read has no relationship to what X wrote.

items.prompt: Two browser tabs run the identical script. Tab A sets `counter = 999`. Tab B reads `counter` and gets `0`. What's the most precise explanation?
choices: Tab B's script has a typo
Tabs run as separate processes (or process-like isolates), each with its own private memory — there was never one shared `counter` to begin with
The browser deliberately hides changes from other tabs for security theater, not a real technical reason
JavaScript variables are always read-only across script re-runs
items.explanation: Each tab's `counter` lives in that tab's own process memory. "Setting it in tab A" and "reading it in tab B" were never operating on the same storage — this is process isolation, the same mechanism that keeps any two unrelated processes from stepping on each other's memory.

items.prompt: A program dereferences a NULL pointer and crashes immediately instead of silently reading garbage data. Why?
choices: NULL is a special CPU instruction that always crashes
Address 0x0 is deliberately left unmapped in the process's page table, so any access to it faults
The compiler inserts a runtime check before every pointer dereference
RAM physically has no data at address 0, so the CPU errors automatically
items.explanation: Leaving 0x0 unmapped is a deliberate OS/loader decision, not a hardware property of RAM — it turns a whole class of bugs (using a pointer before it's set to something real) into an immediate, loud fault instead of a silent read of unrelated memory.
items.reference:
0x0 → unmapped → immediate fault

Why: leaving address 0 unmapped turns a whole class of bugs into a loud, immediate crash instead of a silent bad read.
items.learnMore:
Why NULL crashes instead of returning garbage

A pointer that was never assigned a real value is conventionally set to NULL (address 0). The OS loader deliberately leaves address 0 unmapped in every process's page table — no valid physical page backs it, on purpose.

So when code dereferences a NULL pointer, the MMU tries to translate address 0, fails to find a mapping, and raises a page fault. The kernel sees there's no legitimate reason for this access and delivers SIGSEGV, killing the process (or, in a managed runtime, raising a catchable null-reference error instead).

This is a deliberate design choice, not a law of physics — a different OS could in principle map something at address 0 and let you silently read whatever's there. Unix chose to leave it unmapped specifically because a loud crash at the exact moment of the bad access is far easier to debug than data silently corrupted somewhere downstream.

items.prompt: If the OS instead mapped a real, readable page at address 0x0 (rather than leaving it unmapped), what would change about NULL-pointer bugs?
choices: Nothing — NULL pointer bugs would still crash exactly the same way
They'd become silent — the program would read whatever happens to be at that page instead of crashing, making the bug much harder to notice
The program would run faster, since fewer faults occur
It's not possible for an OS to ever map address 0x0
items.explanation: The crash isn't inherent to the number 0 — it's inherent to that address being unmapped. If it were mapped, a NULL dereference would just read whatever's on that page and keep running with corrupted-looking data, which is strictly worse for debugging than an immediate fault.

Why: leaving address 0 unmapped turns a whole class of bugs into a loud, immediate crash instead of a silent bad read.

items.prompt: Which region of a process's address space holds the compiled machine code, and why is it typically marked read-only?
choices: The heap — code is just data allocated at startup
The text segment — read-only so a bug can't accidentally overwrite the program's own instructions
The stack — code lives alongside the current call frame
The data/bss segment, because it's loaded first
items.explanation: The text segment holds the compiled instructions. Marking it read-only means a stray write (a buffer overrun, a bad pointer) can corrupt data or crash the process, but it can't rewrite the program's own logic on the fly.
items.reference:
⬆️ stack — frames, grows down
↕️ heap — dynamic alloc, grows up
📦 data/bss — globals
🔒 text — code, read-only

Why: each region has a distinct purpose and distinct permissions — text is read-only precisely because code shouldn't be writable at runtime.
items.learnMore:
The four regions and why they're separate

A process's address space isn't one undifferentiated block — it's split into regions because each kind of data has different lifetime and permission needs.

text holds compiled instructions and is mapped read-only (and often execute-only) so a bug can't accidentally overwrite the program's own code. data/bss holds globals and statics — fixed in number, known at compile/link time. heap holds anything allocated at runtime (malloc, new, objects) and can grow or shrink as the program requests more or frees it. stack holds function call frames — return addresses, parameters, locals — and grows and shrinks automatically as functions call and return.

Heap and stack are placed at opposite ends of the same free region specifically so neither one has to be sized up front — they only collide if one of them grows unexpectedly large, which is exactly the stack-overflow / heap-exhaustion failure mode.

items.prompt: A function allocates an object with `new` and another calls itself recursively 1000 times. Which two regions grow to accommodate these, respectively?
choices: Both grow the text segment
The heap grows for the `new` allocation; the stack grows for the recursive calls
The stack grows for the `new` allocation; the heap grows for the recursive calls
Both grow the data/bss segment
items.explanation: Dynamic allocation (`new`, `malloc`) always comes from the heap. Function calls — including recursive ones — push frames onto the stack, one per call, regardless of what the function does internally.

items.prompt: You run the same script twice in two separate terminal windows. What's true of the two resulting processes?
choices: They share one PID since it's the same program
They get distinct PIDs and separate address spaces, even though they're running identical code
The second launch fails because the program is already running
They share memory so any variable change in one is visible in the other
items.explanation: A PID identifies a running instance, not a program. Two launches of the same script are two independent processes with two PIDs and two private address spaces — running the same code doesn't mean sharing anything at runtime.
items.reference:
Every fork() → a brand-new, never-reused (until wraparound) PID

Why: the PID is the OS's unique handle for addressing a specific running process, distinct from any other process ever.
items.learnMore:
PIDs identify processes, not programs

A PID (process ID) names one specific running instance, not the program it's running. Launch the same executable five times and you get five different processes, five different PIDs, five separate address spaces — all sharing the same code on disk but none of the same memory.

The OS uses the PID as the key for everything process-related: sending a signal (kill -9 <pid>), reading its status (/proc/<pid>/... on Linux), or waiting for it to exit (waitpid(pid, ...)). Without a stable per-instance identifier, none of these operations could target a specific running process instead of "some process running this program."

items.prompt: Why does the OS need a PID at all, instead of just letting tools refer to processes by their program name (e.g. "node")?
choices: It doesn't need one — program name is always sufficient
Multiple processes can run the same program simultaneously; a PID is needed to target one specific running instance for operations like sending a signal
PIDs exist only for logging, not for any functional purpose
PIDs are required by the filesystem to name files
items.explanation: Program name is ambiguous the moment more than one instance is running. A PID disambiguates: `kill -9 61278` targets exactly one process, where `kill -9 node` wouldn't even be a valid way to express "the second one I started".

items.prompt: What does it mean, precisely, that a process "believes it owns the entire address space"?
choices: The process actually does own all of physical RAM while it runs
The process's view of memory is a private illusion maintained by the OS/MMU — its virtual addresses have no necessary relationship to what any other process sees
It means the process can read any other process's memory if it tries hard enough
It's a marketing term with no real technical meaning
items.explanation: Virtual memory gives every process the same full private address range to program against, regardless of how many other processes exist or how much physical RAM is actually installed — the OS/MMU handle translating that illusion down to real, shared physical memory behind the scenes.
items.reference:
Every process 'believes' it owns the full address space — the OS/MMU maintains that illusion per process.

Why: the illusion of a full private address space is what lets every process be written as if it's alone on the machine.
items.learnMore:
The virtual memory illusion

Without virtual memory, every program would need to know, at compile time, exactly which physical addresses were free — and no two programs running together could ever pick the same address for anything. That's unworkable at scale.

Virtual memory solves this by giving each process its own full, private view of an address space (e.g. the full 48-bit range on a 64-bit system), regardless of how much physical RAM actually exists or what other processes are doing. The MMU and page tables silently translate each process's virtual addresses to wherever physical RAM the OS actually has available — different for every process, invisible to the program itself.

This is also what makes physical RAM oversubscription and swapping possible: a page marked in a process's page table doesn't even have to be backed by RAM at every moment — it could be on disk, brought in only when actually touched.

items.prompt: A machine has 8GB of physical RAM but is running 20 processes, each with its own large virtual address space. How is this possible?
choices: It isn't — the OS would refuse to start more processes than RAM can fit
Virtual address space is nearly free to reserve; only the pages a process actually touches get backed by real physical RAM
Each process is secretly given only 400MB of virtual address space
The processes silently share one physical address space with no isolation
items.explanation: Reserving virtual address space costs almost nothing — it's bookkeeping in a page table. Physical RAM is only consumed for pages a process actually reads or writes, which is why many processes can each declare a large address space without the machine running out of memory immediately.

items.prompt: Why can't an ordinary process just directly read or write another process's memory, if it wanted to?
choices: It's only prevented by a polite convention that well-behaved programs follow
Hardware access and cross-process memory access require kernel mode; ordinary process code runs in a restricted user mode and must go through system calls the kernel controls
The CPU has no concept of privilege levels — this is purely an OS-level software check
It actually can, but antivirus software usually blocks it
items.explanation: The restriction is enforced by the CPU's privilege levels, not just convention: user-mode code physically cannot execute the instructions needed to touch arbitrary hardware or another process's memory. Every such operation must go through a system call into the trusted kernel, which can and does refuse illegitimate requests.
items.reference:
👤 User mode
your code, restricted
🛡️ Kernel mode
full hardware access

Why: a system call is the only sanctioned door between the two — it's what lets untrusted code request privileged work without granting it direct access.
items.learnMore:
Why user code can't touch hardware directly

If every process could directly manipulate hardware (write raw disk sectors, reprogram the network card, touch another process's memory), no OS-level guarantee — isolation, permissions, scheduling fairness — could be enforced. Any process could simply route around them.

Instead, the CPU itself supports privilege levels. Ordinary application code runs in user mode, where certain instructions and memory regions are off-limits. To do anything that touches shared hardware or global state — open a file, allocate memory, send a network packet — user code issues a system call, a well-defined request that traps into kernel mode, where the OS itself (fully trusted, unrestricted) performs the operation on the process's behalf and returns control.

This is the actual enforcement mechanism behind "a process can't read another process's memory" — it's not merely convention, it's that the only doors to privileged operations are ones the kernel controls and can refuse.

items.prompt: A program calls a function to read a file. What has to happen for that read to actually reach the disk?
choices: The user-mode code reads the disk controller registers directly
The user-mode code issues a system call, trapping into kernel mode, where the OS performs the privileged disk operation and returns the result
Nothing special — file reads never involve the kernel
The program must first request root/administrator access from the user
items.explanation: Any interaction with real hardware — including disk reads — is a privileged operation. The user-mode program can't perform it directly; it has to request it via a system call, which is the sanctioned crossing point into kernel mode where the OS does the actual work.

items.prompt: Why does Unix process creation split into two separate steps — fork() then exec() — instead of one combined "start_process()" call?
choices: Historical accident with no real benefit today
Splitting them lets code run in the child (e.g. redirecting file descriptors) after duplication but before the new program's code takes over
fork() is faster than exec(), so splitting them improves performance
exec() requires superuser permissions and fork() doesn't
items.explanation: The gap between fork() and exec() is exactly where a shell sets up things like output redirection (> file, | pipe) — code the shell controls runs there, in the child, before the child's identity is replaced by the new program.
items.reference:
1️⃣ fork() — duplicate
2️⃣ (redirect fds, etc — only in child)
3️⃣ exec() — replace

Why: splitting the two steps leaves a window where the child can be modified before its identity is replaced.
items.learnMore:
Why fork and exec are two calls, not one

A combined "start_process(path)" call would have no way to let the caller customize the child's environment before the new program takes over — file descriptor redirection, changing the working directory, dropping privileges, all of it would have to be built into that one call's API, or be impossible.

By splitting fork (duplicate) from exec (replace), the code that runs between them — still the old program, still able to call ordinary functions — has a window to modify only the child's state: closing/reopening file descriptors, changing environment variables, chrooting, before calling exec to become the new program. This is exactly how a shell implements >, <, and | — none of it needs special-casing inside exec itself.

`fork()` without `exec()` is also independently useful — some servers fork to handle a request in a child running the same code, no new program involved at all.

items.prompt: A shell runs `node app.js > out.log`. At what point does the redirection to `out.log` actually get set up?
choices: Before fork() is called, in the shell's own process
In the child, after fork() returns 0 but before exec() replaces the child's program
Inside exec() itself, as a built-in feature of every program
After exec() completes, by the newly-running node process
items.explanation: The redirection has to happen to the child only, and it has to happen before the child becomes a different program — which is precisely the window between fork() returning in the child and exec() being called. Doing it before fork() would also redirect the shell's own output.

items.prompt: What is `fork()` useful for on its own, without ever calling `exec()` afterward?

items.prompt: A parent process has a 2GB heap. It calls fork(). Does the kernel immediately copy all 2GB into the new child?
choices: Yes, always — that's the whole point of fork()
No — pages start out shared (copy-on-write); a physical copy of a page only happens the instant either process writes to it
No — the child simply shares the parent's memory forever with no copying ever
It depends on whether the child calls exec() afterward
items.explanation: Copy-on-write makes fork() cheap regardless of heap size: pages are shared read-only at first, and only the specific page that gets written is actually duplicated, at the moment of the write — not the whole address space up front.
items.reference:
fork() → pages start shared → first write → real copy made (that page only)

Why: copy-on-write defers the cost of duplicating memory until a write actually happens, and only for the page that changed.
items.learnMore:
Copy-on-write: cheap fork(), true isolation

If `fork()` had to physically copy every byte of the parent's memory immediately, forking a process with a large heap would be slow every single time — even though most fork+exec sequences immediately discard that copied memory the moment exec() replaces it.

Instead, the kernel makes fork() cheap by not copying anything up front: it duplicates the page table (pointers to memory), marking every page in both processes' tables as read-only and copy-on-write. Both processes' pages point at the same physical memory initially. The instant either process writes to one of those pages, the CPU traps the write, the kernel makes a real physical copy of just that one page, updates the writer's page table to point at the new copy, and lets the write proceed.

The result: fork() is fast (near-O(1) regardless of heap size), and isolation still holds perfectly — a write by one process is invisible to the other, because by the time any write happens, they're no longer sharing that page.

items.prompt: Right after fork(), before either process has written anything, what's true about the parent's and child's memory?
choices: They already point at completely separate physical pages
They point at the same physical pages, both marked read-only/copy-on-write, until one of them writes
The child has no memory at all until exec() is called
The parent's memory is temporarily frozen until the child exits
items.explanation: Immediately after fork(), the two processes share physical pages for efficiency — no copying has happened yet. The pages are marked copy-on-write specifically so a later write by either side triggers a real, private copy at that moment, not before.
items.reference:
fork() → pages start shared → first write → real copy made (that page only)

Why: copy-on-write defers the cost of duplicating memory until a write actually happens, and only for the page that changed.

Both processes' pages point at the same physical memory initially. The instant either process writes to one of those pages, the CPU traps the write, the kernel makes a real physical copy of just that one page, updates the writer's page table to point at the new copy, and lets the write proceed.

The result: fork() is fast (near-O(1) regardless of heap size), and isolation still holds perfectly — a write by one process is invisible to the other, because by the time any write happens, they're no longer sharing that page.

items.prompt: What hardware component performs the virtual-to-physical address translation on every memory access, and what does it consult to do it?
choices: The disk controller, consulting the filesystem
The MMU, consulting the current process's page table
The CPU's L1 cache, consulting a hash of the process name
The OS scheduler, consulting the process's priority
items.explanation: The MMU (memory management unit) is dedicated CPU hardware for this exact purpose — it translates every virtual address a running process touches into a physical one, by looking it up in that process's page table.
items.reference:
virtual addr → MMU (via page table) → physical addr

Why: the MMU consults the current process's page table on every memory access — there is no path that skips this.
items.learnMore:
Page tables and the MMU, mechanically

A page table is a per-process data structure the kernel maintains, mapping ranges of virtual addresses ("pages") to ranges of physical addresses ("frames"). The CPU has dedicated hardware, the MMU, whose job is to consult the currently-active process's page table on every single memory access and perform this translation, transparently to the running code.

When the scheduler context-switches from one process to another, part of that switch is telling the MMU which page table to use next — this is why a context switch is more expensive than it might look: it can invalidate cached translations (the TLB, a small cache of recent translations) and force the CPU to re-walk the new process's page table on its next several memory accesses.

A page table entry can also simply be absent or marked invalid — which is exactly the case for address 0x0 in every process (the deliberate NULL-guard) and for any address a process hasn't been given any mapping for at all.

items.prompt: What triggers the heap to grow, versus what triggers the stack to grow?
choices: Both grow automatically on a fixed timer
The heap grows when code explicitly requests more memory (malloc/new); the stack grows implicitly, one frame per function call

items.explanation: Heap growth is explicit and request-driven — an allocator asks the OS for more address space when it runs low. Stack growth is implicit and automatic — every function call adds a frame with no explicit "grow the stack" call from the programmer.

📈 heap

📉 stack

Why: heap growth is explicit (you ask for it); stack growth is implicit (it happens as a side effect of calling a function).
items.learnMore:
Two different growth mechanisms, one shared risk

The heap grows only when code explicitly asks for more memory (`malloc`, `new`, appending to a dynamic array that needs to reallocate). The allocator tracks free and used blocks and, when it runs out of already-reserved space, asks the OS (via a system call like `brk`/`mmap`) for more virtual address space to manage.

The stack grows implicitly: every function call pushes a new frame — return address, parameters, local variables — with zero explicit action from the programmer. Most OSes let the stack grow on demand up to a configured limit (checked via `ulimit -s` on Linux) rather than reserving its maximum size up front.

Both mechanisms share the same underlying risk: if either one grows without bound (an allocator that never frees, a recursive function with no reachable base case), it eventually exhausts either the available memory or the reserved stack region — heap exhaustion and stack overflow are the same category of failure, arrived at from opposite directions.

items.prompt: Put these in the correct order for how a segfault actually happens: (a) kernel delivers SIGSEGV, (b) code accesses an invalid virtual address, (c) MMU raises a page fault, (d) kernel's page-fault handler finds no valid mapping
choices: a, b, c, d
b, c, d, a
c, b, a, d
d, c, b, a
items.explanation: The access happens first (b), which the MMU can't translate so it faults (c), the kernel's handler inspects the fault and finds no legitimate mapping (d), and only then does it deliver the fatal signal (a) — a segfault is the end of a pipeline, not a single instantaneous event.
items.reference:
bad access → MMU page fault → kernel checks mapping → none found → SIGSEGV

Why: a segfault is the kernel's considered response to an access it has no valid mapping for, not a hardware malfunction.
items.learnMore:
The segfault pipeline, step by step

When code accesses a virtual address, the MMU tries to translate it using the current page table. If there's no valid entry for that address (unmapped, or mapped with permissions that forbid the attempted operation — e.g. writing to the read-only text segment), the MMU raises a page fault, trapping into the kernel.

The kernel's page-fault handler then has to decide what this fault means. Some page faults are entirely normal and handled silently — e.g. a page that's valid but not yet backed by physical RAM (lazily allocated, or swapped out to disk), which the kernel just backs and lets the process continue. But if the faulting address has no valid mapping at all for this process — the classic "this pointer points nowhere" case — the kernel concludes the access is illegitimate and delivers `SIGSEGV` to the process, whose default handler terminates it.

This is why "segfault" specifically means an access to genuinely unmapped/forbidden memory, not any memory-related slowness or error — a page fault that resolves successfully (lazy allocation, swap-in) never becomes a segfault at all.

items.prompt: L3 showed a stack limit turning unbounded recursion into a catchable error rather than a silent runaway. Write willStackOverflow(currentDepth, frameSizeBytes, stackLimitBytes) that returns true once the recursion would exceed the stack's size.

tests.description: exactly at the limit is not yet an overflow
one frame past the limit overflows

items.explanation: This is the same arithmetic the runtime is implicitly doing when it decides to throw "Maximum call stack size exceeded": total space used so far (depth × cost per frame) compared against the reserved stack size. It's `>` and not `>=` because using exactly the full budget hasn't overflowed it yet — the next frame would.
items.reference:
depth × frame size vs stack limit

Why: this is literally the arithmetic a runtime does internally before deciding to throw a stack-overflow error.
items.learnMore:
The arithmetic behind a stack-overflow guard

A managed runtime (like JS's V8) doesn't wait for the OS to segfault it — it tracks roughly how much stack space has been consumed and compares that against a configured limit, throwing a catchable error once the budget would be exceeded.

The comparison is simple: how many frames deep is the current call (depth), multiplied by roughly how much space each frame costs (which varies by how many locals/parameters a function has), compared against the total reserved stack size. Once that product would exceed the limit, the runtime throws rather than letting the next call actually run — this is what `L3-deep-dive.md`'s `stack.mjs` example is demonstrating happening automatically.

Using exactly the full budget (`depth * frameSize === limit`) hasn't overflowed yet — the next single frame would be what pushes it over, so the boundary condition matters: strictly greater-than, not greater-or-equal.

Return { parent, child } where parent is unchanged and child has the writes applied on top of a copy of parentMemory.

tests.description: keys not in writes are inherited from the parent in the child
tests.expr: expect(forkAndWrite({ a: 1, b: 2 }, { a: 99 }).child).toEqual({ a: 99, b: 2 })

tests.description: mutating the returned child does not affect the returned parent object
tests.expr: const r = forkAndWrite({ x: 1 }, { x: 2 }); r.child.x = 500; expect(r.parent.x).toBe(1)

items.explanation: This mirrors fork_isolation.py's actual behavior: the parent's memory is never touched, and the child gets a full logical copy with only its own writes layered on top — exactly what copy-on-write guarantees at the OS level, just modeled here with a plain object spread instead of real page tables.
items.reference:
write → copy that page only → diverge

Why: modeling copy-on-write as 'copy on first write, share until then' captures the real kernel behavior from fork_isolation.py.
items.learnMore:
Modeling copy-on-write in code

`fork_isolation.py` in L3 showed real copy-on-write behavior: parent and child start with identical values, and a write in one is invisible to the other. The underlying rule the kernel implements is: pages start shared, and a physical copy of a page is made lazily, only for the process that writes to it, only at the moment it writes.

Modeling this in ordinary code (without real OS pages) means treating 'the child's view' as a copy that only diverges from the parent's once the child writes — before any write, reading from either side should see the same values, exactly mirroring what the real `fork()` guarantees.

Reading /proc/self/maps lines

Each line of `/proc//maps` on Linux describes one contiguous virtual memory region for that process: the address range (`start-end` in hex), permissions (`rwxp` or similar), file offset, device, inode, and optionally a name (a file path, or a bracketed pseudo-name like `[heap]` or `[stack]`).

Parsing these lines programmatically is a real, practical skill — tools that inspect a process's memory layout (debuggers, profilers, security scanners checking for unexpected writable+executable regions) all start from exactly this format.

items.learnMore:
Tracking heap growth over time

L3's `heap.mjs` proved the heap grows by snapshotting `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` before and after a large allocation and comparing the two numbers. That same before/after-delta technique generalizes to tracking memory growth across any sequence of operations — which is exactly what a memory profiler or a leak-detection tool does under the hood, just automated and sampled continuously instead of at two manually-chosen points.

A useful derived signal from a series of such snapshots is whether usage is trending upward without ever coming back down — that pattern (monotonically increasing, never released) is the practical signature of a leak, as opposed to normal allocate/free churn that goes up and down but stays roughly flat over time.

stackLimitKB × 1024 ÷ frameSize = maxDepth

items.learnMore:
Frame size, stack size, and safe recursion depth

The interactive demo on this unit lets you drag both a per-frame cost and a total stack size to see how deep a recursion can go before overflowing. The relationship is direct division: more bytes per frame (more local variables, more parameters) means fewer frames fit in the same stack budget; a larger configured stack size (raised via `ulimit -s` on Linux, for example) means more frames fit for the same per-frame cost.

This is a real, practical lever: a recursive algorithm that's "fine" in testing with small inputs can blow the stack in production with larger inputs, and the fix isn't always 'raise the stack limit' — sometimes it's restructuring the recursion to use less state per frame, or converting it to an iterative loop that uses the heap (or no extra memory at all) instead of the stack.

items.explanation: Every process (besides the very first) has a parent, tracked by PPID — grouping processes by their ppid reconstructs the same tree structure `pstree` shows on a real machine, just from raw { pid, ppid } records instead of reading them live from the kernel.

shell (PID 100) → fork → child (PID 101) → fork → grandchild (PID 102)

Why: pids.mjs showed a real parent/child PID pair — a process tree is just that relationship extended across multiple generations.
items.learnMore:
Process trees and PPIDs

Every process (except the kernel's very first one, PID 1 / init) has a parent — the process whose fork() created it. The OS tracks this as the PPID (parent PID), and the full set of these relationships across every running process forms a tree, visible on Linux via `ps --forest` or `pstree`.

This tree matters operationally: killing a parent doesn't automatically kill its children (they get "re-parented" to init/PID 1 and keep running as orphans, unless the parent explicitly waits for and manages them), and a parent that never calls `wait()` on an exited child leaves it as a zombie — an entry in the process table with no running code, just exit-status bookkeeping the parent never collected.

items.prompt: Write isExecutable(permString) that returns true if a /proc/self/maps permission string like 'rw-p' or 'r-xp' indicates the region is executable (the third character is 'x', not '-').
items.explanation: The permission string is always four characters in a fixed order (read, write, execute, shared/private) — checking index 2 for 'x' tells you whether code is allowed to run from that region at all, which is exactly the distinction that makes text executable but heap/stack (correctly) not.
items.reference:
rwxp → read / write / execute / private-or-shared

Why: text is r-x (readable+executable, not writable); heap/stack are rw- (readable+writable, not executable) — the permission bits enforce exactly the boundaries L1/L2 described.
items.learnMore:
What the permission letters in /proc/self/maps mean

Each maps line's permission field is four characters: read, write, execute, and shared-or-private. A region marked `r-xp` (like the text segment) can be read and executed but not written — this is the hardware-enforced version of "code shouldn't be writable at runtime" from L1. A region marked `rw-p` (like heap and stack) can be read and written but not executed — this is also a real security boundary: it's what stops a classic buffer-overflow exploit from simply writing shellcode onto the stack and jumping to it, since the stack's pages aren't executable.

The trailing `p` vs `s` indicates private (copy-on-write, this process's own eventual copy) vs shared (genuinely shared physical memory, e.g. a shared library's code mapped into multiple processes at once).

items.prompt: Write isSuspiciousRegion(permString) that flags a region as suspicious if it's BOTH writable and executable at the same time (position 1 is 'w' AND position 2 is 'x') — a real red flag security scanners look for, since legitimate regions are almost never both.
items.explanation: A writable+executable (W^X-violating) region is unusual precisely because it defeats the protection this pool's reference explains: if code can be written and then executed from the same page, an attacker who can write arbitrary bytes there can run arbitrary code — which is exactly why the text segment is r-x and the stack/heap are rw-, never both at once, on a well-configured system.
